# Exploration 2.2 Strawberry Storage

A study (Smith & Skog, “Postharvest Carbon Dioxide Treatment Enhances Firmness of Several Cultivars of Strawberry,” American Society for Horticulture Science, 27(5), 1992) was conducted in order to investigate the effects of storage method on the firmness of strawberries. As strawberries are harvested, they are placed into storage containers called “clamshells.”

Because clamshells have holes in them, air can circulate from outside the clamshell into the clamshell and vice versa while the container still protects the fruit. To test the potential effect of changing the composition of the air in which strawberries are stored, researchers obtained 15 clamshells filled with strawberries of several different varieties. Five clamshells were randomly assigned to be stored in regular air (approximately 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide) and five clamshells were randomly assigned to be stored in a modified air method (18% oxygen and 15% carbon dioxide). After two days of refrigeration at 0.5°C in one of the two different atmospheres, the strawberries were then left at room temperature in regular air for two more days. The firmness of the strawberries was then measured by the force (measured in newtons, N) needed for a probe to pierce the exterior of the strawberry. The remaining five clamshells were randomly assigned to a “control” condition which measured the strawberries immediately (not after four days like the other two conditions).The data for this study is in `Strawberries` within `library(ImSIwithR)`. Let's load the data.

> a. Calculate the observed effects for each storage method: 

!!! Remove **eval=FALSE** after inserting the path and successfully running the code AND *remove this note*.

```{r, Calculate group means and overall mean, eval=FALSE}
stats <- Strawberries %>%
  summarize(
    grand_mean = mean(Firmness),
    mean_Air = mean(Firmness[Storage == "Air"]),
    mean_Control = mean(Firmness[Storage == "Control"]),
    mean_Mod = mean(Firmness[Storage == "ModifiedAir"])
  )

# Calculate Effects (Group Mean - Grand Mean)
effects <- stats %>%
  transmute(
    Effect_Air = mean_Air - grand_mean,
    Effect_Control = mean_Control - grand_mean,
    Effect_Mod = mean_Mod - grand_mean
  )

print(effects)
```

> 3. Consider a simulated null distribution of the F-statistic produced by R below. How much variation in firmness values is explained by the storage method? Based on the F-statistic and the null distribution, should we find a large p-value or a small p-value? How are you deciding? 

!!! Remove **eval=FALSE** after inserting the path and successfully running the code AND *remove this note*.

```{r, null distribution for the F-statistic, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(1)

# Simulation 1: Completely Randomized (ignoring blocks)
null_distribution_CRD <- do(1000) * aov(Firmness ~ shuffle(Storage), data = Strawberries)

# filter for the F values (drop NA if any)
Fstat_CRD <- null_distribution_CRD %>% filter(!is.na(F))

# summary stats for null distribution
null_mean <- mean(Fstat_CRD$F)
null_sd   <- sd(Fstat_CRD$F)

# one-way ANOVA model
model_storage <- aov(Firmness ~ Storage, data = Strawberries)
# observed F 
obs_F <- summary(model_storage)[[1]]["Storage", "F value"]

# formatted label
label_text <- paste0(
  "Null mean = ", round(null_mean, 3), "\n",
  "Null SD   = ", round(null_sd, 3), "\n",
  "Observed F= ", round(obs_F, 3), "\n")

# plot with annotation in the top-right
ggplot(Fstat_CRD, aes(x = F)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "skyblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_F, color = "red", size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Simulated Null Distribution of F-statistics (CRD)",
       x = "F-statistic",
       y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal() +
  annotate("text", x = Inf, y = Inf, label = label_text,
           hjust = 1.05, vjust = 1.1, size = 3.8)
```

## Blocking Decision: 

Rather than limiting themselves to one type of strawberry (i.e., using inclusion criteria of one type of strawberry) which would most likely have given them a smaller *SSError*, the researchers decided to include five different varieties of strawberries in the study allowing them to generalize to a more diverse population of strawberries. Suspecting that different varieties of strawberries have different firmness ratings, that is, believing variety is associated with firmness (the response variable), the researchers opted to block on strawberry variety. In this way the variation explained by variety will be accounted for in the analysis by removing it from the unexplained variation.

## Key Idea: RCBD (Randomized Complete Block Design)


To start, samples of harvested Allstar strawberries were randomly placed into three clamshells and each clamshell was then randomly assigned to one of the three storage methods. This procedure was implemented for the four remaining strawberry varieties, as well. This restricted random assignment guarantees that there is one clamshell of each variety for each storage method. See the diagram for an illustration of this random assignment process.

!!! Change the path and remove **eval=FALSE** after uploading the Strawberry Diagram to Server and updating the path  .

```{r include_image, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Number of ways to pick items", out.width="80%", fig.align="center",eval=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("~/Documents/Math 248 Materials/Math 248 Resources/ISI2 Math 248/Strawberry Diagram.png")
```

The experimental unit in this study is the clamshell, not the individual strawberries because the treatments were assigned to the clamshells.

A _block study design_ creates _blocks of experimental units that are similar to each other-, randomly assigns the treatments _within each block-, and then analyzes the data in a way which accounts for _block-to-block variations_. 

When there are _only two groups being compared a block study design is called a matched pairs design-. The term block comes from the first block designs which were agricultural experiments in large fields where separate parts of the field were called “blocks.”


## Modifying the Analysis to Consider Blocking

Now that we know more about the actual way this study was designed, we know that an analysis that ignores this “restricted randomization” is incorrect. Instead, the analysis should reflect the study design that was used.

## Key Idea:

**The data analysis should correspond to the study’s design.**

_Because the study design was actually a randomized complete block design, we need to re-consider how to simulate the behavior of the F-statistic assuming the null hypothesis to be true._

# Analysis 2: Revising the F-statistic to Account for Blocking

!!! Remove **eval=FALSE** after inserting the path and successfully running the code AND *remove this note*.

```{r, ANOVA table for RCBD model, eval=FALSE}
model_variety_storage <- aov(Firmness ~ Variety + Storage, data = Strawberries)
anova(model_variety_storage)
```

> 9. Explain how each degrees of freedom value is calculated in the ANOVA table above.

> 10. What percentage of the variation in the response is due to the blocking variable and what percentage is due to the storage method? What does this say about the importance of this blocking variable in this study? 

!!! Remove **eval=FALSE** after inserting the path and successfully running the code AND *remove this note*.

```{r, proportion of explained variation calculation, eval=FALSE}
# ANOVA table (type I sums of squares - sequential sums of squares)
anova_tab <- anova(model_variety_storage)

# total sum of squares about the grand mean (explicit, handles NAs)


# proportions for terms (student, chiptype, Residual)
term_SS <- c(variety_explained_variability = anova_tab["Variety", "Sum Sq"],
             storage_explained_variability = anova_tab["Storage", "Sum Sq"],
             Residual = anova_tab["Residuals", "Sum Sq"])

SS_total <-anova_tab["Variety", "Sum Sq"]+anova_tab["Storage", "Sum Sq"]+anova_tab["Residuals", "Sum Sq"]
  
prop_term <- term_SS / SS_total

# results
prop_term         # proportion of total SS explained by each term
```

### Important Note:

_We conducted two analyses (one that considered the blocking design and one that did not) on the same data in order to illustrate the benefits of blocking. In practice, we analyze data only in a manner that reflects the study design. Using multiple analysis methods on the same data did help to clarify for us just how important consideration of the blocking variable is in this case._

Because the actual study used blocking and we modified the analysis to account for the blocking variable, we need to modify the null and alternative hypothesis being tested as shown here.

**Null hypothesis** $H_0$: The long-run average firmness of strawberries in each of the three experimental conditions is the same, after accounting for differences in firmness between different varieties of strawberries.

**Alternative hypothesis**  $H_a$: At least one of the three experimental conditions have a different long-run average firmness of strawberries, after accounting for differences in firmness between different varieties of strawberries.

##: Validity conditions for ANOVA with a blocking variable

Recall that theory-based approaches like those you have been using require certain validity conditions to be met. Here are the validity conditions for ANOVA with a blocking variable.


### The F-distribution is a good approximation to the null distribution of the F-statistic as long as:

- Either the sample size is at least 20 for each of the groups being compared, without skewness or outliers; *or* if the sample sizes are less than 20 for each group, then the distribution of adjusted response variable within each group is approximately symmetric. 

- The standard deviations of the adjusted response variable samples in each group being compared are approximately equal to each other. (Largest SD is not more than twice the smallest SD)

- The experimental units are randomly assigned to the treatments within each block.


> 14. Comment on how the analysis you just conducted meets the validity conditions by evaluating the three conditions listed in the Validity conditions box.

!!! Remove **eval=FALSE** after inserting the path and successfully running the code AND *remove this note*.

```{r, adjusted response variable in each group, eval=FALSE}
#calculate overall mean
overall_mean <- mean(Strawberries$Firmness)

#summarize and calculate blocking effect. 
block_effects <- Strawberries %>%
  group_by(Variety) %>%
  summarize(
    variety_mean = mean(Firmness),
    block_effect = variety_mean - overall_mean
  )

# Join effects back to main data and calculate adjusted firmness
Strawberries <- Strawberries %>%
  left_join(block_effects, by = "Variety") %>%
  mutate(Firmness_Adj = Firmness - block_effect)

FirmSD<- sd(Strawberries$Firmness)
FirmSD_Adj<-sd(Strawberries$Firmness_Adj)

#look for skewness and outliers or approximately symmetric
ggplot(Strawberries, aes(x = Storage, y = Firmness_Adj, fill= Storage)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Adjusted Firmness by Storage")
```

!!! Remove **eval=FALSE** after inserting the path and successfully running the code AND *remove this note*.

```{r, check standard deviations, eval=FALSE}
#
Strawberries %>%
  group_by(Storage) %>%
  summarize(sd_adj = sd(Firmness_Adj))
```
